canonical_topic: Why crude oil is transported unrefined to its destination
definition: Crude oil is shipped in its raw form and only refined near its final destination, a business model driven by refinery economics, labor availability, local demand/regulatory optimization, and safety/political risk.
core_idea: Refineries are multibillion-dollar, multi-decade assets that outlive any single oil field, need a skilled workforce best found near cities, benefit from being close to the customers whose demand/regulations they must match, and are sited for safety and political stability — all of which favor building refineries near demand rather than near the oil field.
key_points: Refineries can cost billions of dollars and have expected lifespans over 50 years, so a refinery typically outlives any single oil field feeding it.
Oil fields are often in remote locations, while refineries need a highly trained workforce more easily found near major cities.
Refineries sited near their customers can tailor output to local demand and comply with local regulations.
Refineries are also sited to protect worker and investor safety, including avoiding locations at risk of violence or nationalization by unfriendly governments.
relationships: This logistics pattern explains why crude oil, rather than refined products, moves via pipeline and ship over long distances
trading_implications: Refinery location decisions (near demand centers, in stable jurisdictions) shape regional crude oil flows and can be a factor in long-term crude transportation/logistics analysis.
